answer: Answer (hypothesis): Economics is the domain in which the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies. In the dataset of 141 original/replication pairs, Economics studies have majority-male authorship in the original study for 77.8% of pairs and in the replication for 72.2% of pairs — both far above Social (57.8% / 48.4%) and Cognitive (67.3% / 44.9%) — and 55.6% of Economics pairs are majority-male on BOTH sides, versus 36.7% for Cognitive and 26.6% for Social. The mean male-author ratio in Economics is 0.870 (original) and 0.837 (replication), versus ~0.66–0.71 and ~0.50–0.52 in the other disciplines. This ranking is robust to every sensitivity check performed (including/excluding drop==True pairs, tie-inclusive ≥0.5 threshold, and a mean-of-lab-rows alternative for replication authorship), so the headline is robust, not a silent choice.

payload.hypothesis: Economics is the domain in which the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies: 55.6% of Economics O/R pairs have majority-male authorship on both sides (mean male ratio 0.870 original, 0.837 replication), versus Cognitive (36.7%) and Social (26.6%); the ranking is robust to threshold, drop-flag and replication-authorship-aggregation sensitivities.
payload.workflow: Loaded meta-regression_study_data (927 rows, 57 cols); deduplicated to 141 O/R pairs using aggregated==True rows for ml1/ml3 and the single rows for rpp/ee; verified 0 missing values in authors_male.o/r; primary analysis excluded drop==True pairs; classified each pair majority-male if authors_male ratio > 0.5 for both original and replication; aggregated shares and means per discipline; ran sensitivities (include drop==True, >=0.5 tie-inclusive threshold, mean-of-lab-rows replication authorship for ml1/ml3). Second dataset (143 rows, effect sizes/p-values only, no authorship/discipline) excluded. Economics wins under all scenarios.
